children: UBS says overall housing-market risks remain broadly stable, but AI-driven wealth, tight supply and stretched affordability are creating sharper divides within and between major cities.

Zurich and Tokyo are the only major cities facing a “high” risk of a housing bubble in 2026, while Miami ranks as the most vulnerable U.S. market, according to the latest UBS Global Real Estate Bubble Index.

Zurich leads the 23-city index with a score of 1.69, followed by Tokyo at 1.54. UBS classifies scores above 1.5 as high risk. Miami ranks third globally at 1.41, placing it in the elevated-risk category alongside Dubai, Seoul, Geneva and Lisbon.
Los Angeles, Sydney, Frankfurt, Toronto, Vancouver, Munich, Hong Kong, Singapore and Milan carry moderate risk. Paris, London, New York, San Francisco and São Paulo are classified as low risk.

Overall bubble risks have changed little from 2025. Inflation-adjusted home prices, rents and incomes were broadly flat over the past year, while financing costs edged higher. Housing shortages in many cities continue to provide support for prices despite worsening affordability.

For property investors, the report points to an increasingly fragmented global market. High borrowing costs are restraining demand, but limited supply and wealth creation are supporting prices in selected cities. That makes local economic conditions, housing supply and exposure to wealthy buyers increasingly important in determining returns.
AI wealth reshapes housing markets
UBS highlighted the growing role of financial wealth in housing demand as homeownership becomes less affordable for households dependent primarily on wages.

Strong equity markets have increased the purchasing power of affluent buyers, while the AI investment boom is creating concentrated pockets of new wealth. UBS said this is helping prime residential properties outperform broader markets, with the divide particularly visible in San Francisco and Seoul.

The trend could make some housing markets less responsive to the traditional interest-rate cycle. Cities that capture a large share of AI investment may benefit from stronger wages, productivity gains and rising household wealth.

At the same time, geopolitical uncertainty and inflation concerns could support demand for properties in markets viewed as safe havens, particularly cities with political stability and a supply of trophy assets.

UBS cautioned that the concentration of wealth is complicating traditional measures of housing risk. Prices in prime neighborhoods can increasingly diverge from local incomes and the broader housing market. Lower reliance on borrowing among wealthy buyers may reduce financial-system risks even as affordability deteriorates for other households.
Home-price growth slows
Across the cities studied, inflation-adjusted home prices rose an average of just 0.5% over the past four quarters, slowing from 1.4% in mid-2025.

Seoul was the strongest market, with real prices rising more than 10%, helped by an AI-driven economic expansion. Lisbon and Madrid also posted strong gains. Hong Kong rebounded sharply, while Tokyo recorded real price growth of 6%.

At the other end of the spectrum, Toronto and Vancouver saw real prices fall around 10%. Prices in Frankfurt and Munich declined almost 4%. Most U.S. cities also recorded negative real price growth, with San Francisco the exception.

The divergence is even greater when markets are grouped by bubble risk. In cities carrying high or elevated risk, real home prices have risen almost 30% on average over the past five years. Rents rose 15% and incomes increased only about 8%. Home prices in moderate- and low-risk cities declined nearly 10% over the same period.
Miami boom loses momentum
Miami remains an outlier among U.S. cities despite signs that its property boom is cooling.

Over the past 15 years, Miami recorded the strongest inflation-adjusted housing appreciation of any city in the study. Home prices tripled while household incomes rose only 25%. More recently, high borrowing costs have pressured demand and real home prices declined over the past year.

UBS said conditions differ sharply by property type. Single-family housing inventories remain tight, while condominium supply is higher and units are taking longer to sell. Mandatory building inspections, reserve requirements and rising insurance premiums have also increased the cost of owning older condos.

UBS nevertheless sees support from people relocating from higher-cost and higher-tax states. Miami's luxury market has also proved more resilient because a large share of purchases are made with cash, reducing sensitivity to mortgage rates.

New York carries a bubble-risk score of just 0.28, while San Francisco's score is negative at -0.02. Los Angeles ranks higher at 0.69, putting it in the moderate-risk category. UBS noted that its figures for all three cities were adjusted because of revisions to source data.
Buying remains expensive compared with renting
Affordability remains a major constraint across global cities.

A skilled service worker would need roughly 15 years of average income to buy a 60-square-meter, or about 650-square-foot, apartment near Hong Kong's city center. Price-to-income ratios exceed 10 in Tokyo, Paris, London and Seoul. UBS also considers affordability stretched in cities including Singapore, Lisbon, Zurich, Geneva and New York.
Compared with 2021, a typical skilled service worker can afford about one-third less living space because of the combination of prices and higher financing costs.

The investment case also looks challenging when property values are compared with rents. Zurich has the highest price-to-rent ratio at 46, meaning 46 years of rental income would be needed to equal the purchase price of a comparable apartment. Geneva follows at 40, while Munich, Frankfurt and Hong Kong have ratios above 30.

Direct ownership expenses, including mortgage interest, maintenance, taxes, depreciation and the opportunity cost of equity, exceed rents for comparable properties in every city in the study. UBS said this means the financial argument for buying often depends heavily on expectations that home prices will continue to rise.
Higher rates remain the key pressure point

UBS expects elevated financing costs to continue weighing on housing prices in the near term. In most cities, the direct cost of owning a 650-square-foot home exceeds 40% of a highly skilled worker's income.

Still, the bank sees persistent housing shortages providing longer-term support. Rents have generally matched or exceeded income growth during the past five years, suggesting that underlying demand for urban housing remains firm.

UBS stressed that its index measures the risk of substantial housing-market mispricing rather than forecasting a crash. A high score does not indicate when or whether prices will fall. Changes in interest rates, investor sentiment or housing supply could ultimately determine whether stretched valuations result in a correction.

title: Zurich and Tokyo top UBS housing bubble risk index as global price growth slows
